note.title: On the cutting of velvet at dusk, and the patience it asks of the hand.
note.p1: The first cut is never the deepest. We learned this from an aunt — who learned it from her own — that velvet asks for the slow knife, the one that waits for the nap to settle before it commits. The maison was built around small lessons of this kind: that a wax seal cools in under a minute but holds for a century, that an iris will refuse to open if you watch it too closely, that a watch crown is best turned with the ball of the thumb, not the nail.
note.p2: None of this is on our website by accident. Each object you’ll find here has been refused, redrafted, and accepted by hands that have argued about it. We are a small house. We prefer it this way.

atelier.metaDescription: The craft, materials and philosophy behind Sanguine — a house built on slow work and deliberate beauty.
atelier.kicker: The House Atelier · Dhaka · Est. MMXXVI
atelier.lede: A workshop built on the conviction that beautiful things deserve to be made slowly.
atelier.s1p1: The maison was assembled in a narrow room in Dhaka — not a studio, exactly; more like the back of a thought. A cluster of objects that refused to coexist anywhere else: a folded length of muga silk, a bottle of vetiver absolute, a bound notebook with marbled covers. The first collection was not designed so much as gathered.
atelier.s1p2: We did not set out to build a brand. We set out to answer a question: what would a house of beautiful things look like if it were built in Bangladesh, with Bangladeshi hands, for people who had always been told that beauty was an import?
atelier.s2p1: We work principally in fabrics that have waiting built into them. Muslin, voile, velvet — textiles that ask the cutter to slow down, that punish haste with puckering and reward quiet with drape. Our weavers source from mills in Cumilla and Khulna, where the looms are still hand-warped and the pace is set by the warp, not the schedule.
atelier.s2Quote: Velvet asks for the slow knife. The one that waits for the nap to settle before it commits.
atelier.s2p2: Our perfumes begin with attars — thick, resinous concentrates pressed from rose, oud, sandalwood and vetiver — and are built outward from there rather than downward from a brief. The iris in our spring eau was macerated for eleven days past what any formula required.
atelier.s3p1: There is a certain kind of deliberateness that looks, from a distance, like inefficiency. It is the florist who ties a ribbon three times before it is right. The perfumer who lets a maceration sit a week past the minimum. The bookbinder who chooses the cloth before the title. We take this as instruction.
atelier.s3p2: We produce limited quantities for a reason that is not strategic: we cannot make more without compromising what we make. Each season’s output is bounded by what a small team can do with full attention, and we consider that boundary a feature, not a constraint.
atelier.s3Quote: A wax seal cools in under a minute but holds for a century. We are interested in that ratio.
atelier.s4p1: The maison is small by design. Our core team — cutters, a perfumer, a bookbinder, and two florists — works from the same address in Gulshan. We do not outsource what can be done in this room. Everything that leaves carrying a wax seal has been touched, in some way, by someone whose name we know.
atelier.s4p2: We pay wages above market, offer flexible hours, and close for the full week of Eid. We consider these facts unremarkable — simply the conditions under which good work is possible.
atelier.ctaText: The pieces speak for themselves better than we can.

journal.i1Title: On the cutting of velvet at dusk, and the patience it asks of the hand
journal.i1Excerpt: The first cut is never the deepest. We learned this from an aunt — who learned it from her own — that velvet asks for the slow knife, the one that waits for the nap to settle before it commits.
journal.i2Title: The iris will not open if you watch it too closely
journal.i2Excerpt: There is something instructive about a flower that refuses to perform on your schedule. The iris opens when it is ready — the arrangement adjusts, not the bloom.
journal.i3Title: A watch that belongs to no one yet finds its owner in the turning of a crown
journal.i3Excerpt: The cabochon crown is the last thing a watchmaker touches. It is the hinge between mechanism and wearer — and it is, quietly, the part that introduces the two.
journal.i4Title: Notes on first editions and the particular smell of their commitment
journal.i4Excerpt: A first edition is not a book so much as a decision — someone chose to hold back a copy at the moment of highest uncertainty. That hesitation, that act of faith, is what you are really buying.
